findings.description: Credentials (usernames, passwords, API keys, tokens, or connection strings) were discovered in plaintext within web-accessible content, including HTML source, JavaScript files, configuration files served by the web server, or directory listing contents. Plaintext credentials in web-accessible content can be harvested by any user who can access the page and frequently provide direct access to backend databases, APIs, or privileged service accounts.
findings._x_remediation: Immediately rotate all exposed credentials. Remove credentials from web-accessible content. Use environment variables or a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) for credential storage. Audit the web server document root for sensitive files. Implement web application firewall rules to prevent configuration file access.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: BEAST
findings.remediation_brief: Disable TLS 1.0 and SSLv3 entirely. Enable TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. Prioritise AEAD cipher suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) which are not susceptible to BEAST. Modern TLS 1.2 with RC4 elimination and GCM prioritisation eliminates the BEAST attack surface.
findings.description: The server is susceptible to the BEAST attack (Browser Exploit Against SSL/TLS, CVE-2011-3389). BEAST exploits a CBC mode initialisation vector (IV) predictability vulnerability in TLS 1.0 and earlier, allowing a man-in-the-middle attacker who can inject chosen plaintext to decrypt CBC-encrypted session data. While the attack requires a network-adjacent attacker and active JavaScript injection in the victim's browser, TLS 1.0 should not be used in modern deployments.
findings.impact: BEAST (Browser Exploit Against SSL/TLS) exploits a vulnerability in TLS 1.0's CBC-mode cipher initialization to decrypt HTTPS cookies and authentication tokens. An attacker with network access can inject chosen plaintext to recover session secrets, enabling session hijacking.
findings._x_remediation: Disable TLS 1.0 and SSLv3 entirely. Enable TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. Prioritise AEAD cipher suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) which are not susceptible to BEAST. Modern TLS 1.2 with RC4 elimination and GCM prioritisation eliminates the BEAST attack surface.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: LUCKY13
findings.remediation_brief: Prioritise and restrict TLS cipher suites to AEAD algorithms (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) which are immune to CBC padding oracle attacks. Disable all CBC mode cipher suites. Enable TLS 1.3 which exclusively uses AEAD ciphers.
findings.description: The server supports CBC mode cipher suites with HMAC-SHA1 or HMAC-MD5, making it potentially susceptible to the LUCKY13 timing attack (CVE-2013-0169). LUCKY13 is a padding oracle attack against CBC-mode TLS that allows an attacker with precise network timing measurements to decrypt recorded TLS session data. The attack requires approximately 2^23 oracle queries per 16 bytes of plaintext decrypted and is primarily a theoretical concern but indicates use of non-AEAD cipher suites.
findings.impact: LUCKY13 (CVE-2013-0169) is a timing side-channel attack against CBC-mode cipher suites in TLS. An attacker with network-level access can recover plaintext from encrypted sessions by measuring processing time differences.
findings._x_remediation: Prioritise and restrict TLS cipher suites to AEAD algorithms (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) which are immune to CBC padding oracle attacks. Disable all CBC mode cipher suites. Enable TLS 1.3 which exclusively uses AEAD ciphers.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: SWEET32
findings.remediation_brief: Disable all 64-bit block cipher suites including 3DES (TRIPLE-DES, 3DES-EDE-CBC-SHA) and Blowfish. Ensure the server's cipher list does not include any cipher containing DES or 3DES. Enable only AES-128 and AES-256 based ciphers with GCM mode.
findings.description: The server supports cipher suites using 64-bit block ciphers (Triple-DES/3DES or Blowfish), making it susceptible to the SWEET32 birthday attack (CVE-2016-2183). After approximately 2^32 blocks (about 32 GB of traffic), an attacker capturing a long-lived TLS session can exploit birthday bound collisions in the CBC mode to recover short, repeated plaintext segments such as HTTP cookies. 3DES-based cipher suites (TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA) should be considered deprecated.
findings.impact: SWEET32 exploits the birthday bound weakness in 64-bit block ciphers (3DES, Blowfish) used in TLS. After capturing approximately 32GB of ciphertext from a long-lived session, an attacker can recover plaintext blocks, potentially exposing session cookies and authentication tokens.
findings._x_remediation: Disable all 64-bit block cipher suites including 3DES (TRIPLE-DES, 3DES-EDE-CBC-SHA) and Blowfish. Ensure the server's cipher list does not include any cipher containing DES or 3DES. Enable only AES-128 and AES-256 based ciphers with GCM mode.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Chain Incomplete
findings.remediation_brief: Reconfigure the TLS server to present the full certificate chain including all required intermediate CA certificates. Obtain the intermediate certificates from the issuing CA and concatenate them with the server certificate in the correct order (leaf first, then intermediates). Verify with: openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -showcerts.
findings.description: The TLS server does not present the full certificate chain during the TLS handshake, omitting one or more intermediate CA certificates. Clients that do not have the intermediate certificate pre-cached will be unable to build a trusted chain to the root CA and will display a certificate error. This indicates a misconfiguration in the server's TLS certificate installation. Some strict clients and mobile browsers do not perform intermediate certificate fetching (AIA chasing) and will fail validation.
findings.impact: An incomplete certificate chain prevents clients from validating the certificate's trust path. Some clients may reject the connection outright, while others silently proceed without full validation, creating inconsistent security posture across the user base.
findings._x_remediation: Reconfigure the TLS server to present the full certificate chain including all required intermediate CA certificates. Obtain the intermediate certificates from the issuing CA and concatenate them with the server certificate in the correct order (leaf first, then intermediates). Verify with: openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -showcerts.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Long Duration
findings.remediation_brief: Replace the certificate with one having a validity period of 398 days or less. Configure automated certificate renewal (ACME/Let's Encrypt or vendor auto-renewal) to ensure certificates are routinely replaced before expiry. For new certificates, request 90-day validity where possible.
findings.description: The TLS certificate has a validity period exceeding 398 days (approximately 13 months). Since September 2020, Apple, Google, and Mozilla enforce a maximum certificate validity of 398 days, and certificates with longer lifetimes will be rejected by current versions of Safari, Chrome, and Firefox. Longer validity periods also increase the exposure window if a private key is compromised, as the certificate cannot be superseded until it expires or is revoked.
findings.impact: Long-lived certificates increase the window of exposure if the private key is compromised. Industry best practice limits certificate lifetime to reduce the impact of key compromise and ensure regular rotation of cryptographic material.
findings._x_remediation: Replace the certificate with one having a validity period of 398 days or less. Configure automated certificate renewal (ACME/Let's Encrypt or vendor auto-renewal) to ensure certificates are routinely replaced before expiry. For new certificates, request 90-day validity where possible.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Missing SAN
findings.remediation_brief: Replace the certificate with one that includes a valid Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension containing the intended hostname(s). All modern CAs issue certificates with SAN by default. If using an internal CA, update the certificate template to include the SAN extension.
findings.description: The TLS certificate does not contain a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension. Since 2017, all major browsers require a SAN to be present and have deprecated reliance on the Common Name (CN) field for hostname validation. Certificates without a SAN will cause certificate validation errors in Chrome, Firefox, and Safari for any hostname validation, even if the CN matches. This is a certificate issuance and lifecycle management deficiency.
findings.impact: A certificate without Subject Alternative Names (SAN) relies solely on the Common Name field for hostname validation. Modern browsers require SAN entries and may reject CN-only certificates, causing service interruptions and security warnings.
findings._x_remediation: Replace the certificate with one that includes a valid Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension containing the intended hostname(s). All modern CAs issue certificates with SAN by default. If using an internal CA, update the certificate template to include the SAN extension.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Serial Number Entropy

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: Digital Certificates

findings.remediation_brief: Replace the certificate if issued by an internal CA with an outdated serial number generation algorithm. Update the internal CA software or configuration to generate serial numbers with at least 64 bits of CSPRNG-sourced entropy. For externally issued certificates, verify the CA is CA/B Forum compliant.
findings.description: The TLS certificate serial number has low entropy, suggesting it was generated with a non-random or predictable serial number algorithm. CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements (Section 7.1) require that certificate serial numbers contain at least 64 bits of unpredictable entropy. Low-entropy serial numbers may indicate an outdated certificate authority or CA software configuration, and in conjunction with other weaknesses can facilitate certificate collision or impersonation attacks.
findings.impact: Low entropy in certificate serial numbers indicates weak random number generation in the issuing CA's infrastructure. This can enable serial number prediction attacks that facilitate certificate forgery.
findings._x_remediation: Replace the certificate if issued by an internal CA with an outdated serial number generation algorithm. Update the internal CA software or configuration to generate serial numbers with at least 64 bits of CSPRNG-sourced entropy. For externally issued certificates, verify the CA is CA/B Forum compliant.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Weak Encryption Method
findings.remediation_brief: Replace the certificate with one using SHA-256 (or stronger) as the signature algorithm and at minimum RSA-2048 or ECDSA P-256 for the public key. Verify the replacement certificate: openssl x509 -in cert.pem -text | grep 'Signature Algorithm'.
findings.description: The TLS certificate uses a weak signature algorithm or public key. This includes SHA-1 signed certificates (deprecated since 2017), RSA keys shorter than 2048 bits, DSA keys shorter than 2048 bits, or Elliptic Curve keys shorter than 224 bits. Certificates signed with SHA-1 are vulnerable to chosen-prefix collision attacks (demonstrated by SHAttered). Certificates with short RSA keys are vulnerable to factorisation attacks given current computational resources.
findings.impact: Certificates signed with weak algorithms (SHA-1, MD5) are vulnerable to collision attacks that allow an attacker to forge a certificate with the same signature, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks that bypass certificate validation entirely.
findings._x_remediation: Replace the certificate with one using SHA-256 (or stronger) as the signature algorithm and at minimum RSA-2048 or ECDSA P-256 for the public key. Verify the replacement certificate: openssl x509 -in cert.pem -text | grep 'Signature Algorithm'.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Session: Long Duration
aliases: SSL/TLS Cipher: No Cipher Order Configured
findings.remediation_brief: Reduce TLS session ticket lifetime to a maximum of 24 hours. Rotate TLS session ticket encryption keys regularly (every 6-12 hours). Set the session cache timeout to a reasonable value. On nginx: ssl_session_timeout 1h; ssl_session_ticket_key rotation should be automated.
findings.description: The TLS server allows session resumption with a session ticket lifetime or session cache timeout exceeding recommended limits (typically more than 24 hours for session tickets or more than 10 hours for session IDs). Long-lived TLS sessions extend the window during which a stolen session ticket or cached session key can be replayed by an attacker to resume a session without re-authenticating. This also limits the effectiveness of forward secrecy when session tickets are encrypted with a long-lived key.
findings.impact: Excessively long TLS session lifetimes increase the window for session resumption attacks and reduce the effectiveness of forward secrecy. Compromised session tickets remain valid for the entire session duration.
findings._x_remediation: Reduce TLS session ticket lifetime to a maximum of 24 hours. Rotate TLS session ticket encryption keys regularly (every 6-12 hours). Set the session cache timeout to a reasonable value. On nginx: ssl_session_timeout 1h; ssl_session_ticket_key rotation should be automated.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Cipher: No Cipher Order Configured
aliases: SSL/TLS Cipher: No Cipher Order Configured
findings.remediation_brief: Enable server-side cipher suite ordering. On Apache: SSLHonorCipherOrder On. On nginx: ssl_prefer_server_ciphers on. Define a strong cipher list that places AEAD ciphers (ECDHE+AESGCM, ECDHE+CHACHA20) first and excludes weak ciphers entirely.
findings.description: The TLS server does not enforce server-side cipher suite ordering, instead accepting the client's preferred cipher suite. Without server-side cipher preference (SSLHonorCipherOrder), a client can negotiate a weak or deprecated cipher suite even if stronger ciphers are available. This allows a downgrade by a malicious client or a MITM that manipulates ClientHello cipher preferences. Server-side ordering ensures the strongest mutually supported cipher is always selected.
findings.impact: Without server-enforced cipher order, the client's cipher preference is used, which may select weaker ciphers over stronger alternatives. An attacker can manipulate the client to negotiate weak ciphers through downgrade attacks.
findings._x_remediation: Enable server-side cipher suite ordering. On Apache: SSLHonorCipherOrder On. On nginx: ssl_prefer_server_ciphers on. Define a strong cipher list that places AEAD ciphers (ECDHE+AESGCM, ECDHE+CHACHA20) first and excludes weak ciphers entirely.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Ciphers: Obsolete Ciphers
aliases: SSL/TLS Cipher: No Cipher Order Configured
findings.remediation_brief: Audit and update the server's cipher suite configuration. Remove all NULL, EXPORT, RC4, MD5, anon, IDEA, and SEED ciphers. Use a tested cipher string such as the Mozilla TLS configuration generator (ssl-config.mozilla.org) set to 'Intermediate' or 'Modern'. Verify the final cipher list with: openssl s_client -connect <host>:443.
findings.description: The TLS server supports one or more obsolete cipher suites that have been removed from TLS 1.3 and marked as prohibited or deprecated by RFC 8996 and NIST SP 800-52r2. Obsolete cipher suites include those using NULL encryption, EXPORT key exchange, RC4, MD5 MACs, anonymous DH (aNULL/eNULL), or IDEA. Support for these ciphers indicates the server has not been hardened against known cryptographic attacks and may be negotiating weak encryption with vulnerable or misconfigured clients.
findings.impact: Obsolete cipher suites such as RC4 and CBC-mode ciphers are vulnerable to known cryptographic attacks including CVE-2013-2566 (RC4 key stream bias) and CVE-2015-2808 (Bar Mitzvah attack). An attacker performing passive traffic capture can recover plaintext from sessions negotiated with these ciphers, compromising the confidentiality of all transmitted data including credentials and session tokens.
findings._x_remediation: Audit and update the server's cipher suite configuration. Remove all NULL, EXPORT, RC4, MD5, anon, IDEA, and SEED ciphers. Use a tested cipher string such as the Mozilla TLS configuration generator (ssl-config.mozilla.org) set to 'Intermediate' or 'Modern'. Verify the final cipher list with: openssl s_client -connect <host>:443.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Vulnerability: Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160)
findings.remediation_brief: Upgrade OpenSSL to version 1.0.1g or later (or 1.0.2 branch). Revoke and replace the server's TLS certificate and private key immediately — the private key must be assumed compromised. Invalidate all active user sessions. Reissue any client certificates if a client PKI is in use.
findings.description: The target server is confirmed vulnerable to Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160). The OpenSSL heartbeat extension does not properly validate the length field in TLS heartbeat requests, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to read up to 64 KB of server process memory per request. Repeated exploitation can expose TLS private keys, session tokens, plaintext credentials, and other sensitive in-memory data without leaving log entries. This vulnerability is distinct from SS3-010 (which covers testssl detection) — this entry is raised when the Scattershot3 Heartbleed probe module independently confirms the vulnerability.
findings.impact: Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) is a critical memory disclosure vulnerability in OpenSSL that allows an attacker to read up to 64KB of server memory per request without authentication or logging. Leaked memory routinely contains private keys, session tokens, and user credentials, enabling complete compromise of the affected server.
findings._x_remediation: Upgrade OpenSSL to version 1.0.1g or later (or 1.0.2 branch). findings.remediation_brief: Upgrade the operating system to a supported version immediately. Any new vulnerability disclosed after the EOL date will remain permanently unpatched on this host, representing an ever-growing attack surface.

findings.title: SSH Vulnerability: {cve_id}
findings.description: ssh-audit matched the SSH server's banner against its built-in CVE database and identified one or more known vulnerabilities affecting the running version of OpenSSH, Dropbear, or Tectia SSH. The CVE ID, CVSS score, and a short description are recorded in the finding Output field; full details are available in the saved ssh-audit JSON report.
findings.impact: Depending on the specific CVE, an attacker may achieve remote code execution, authentication bypass, user enumeration, host-key spoofing, denial of service, or memory disclosure. Banner-matched CVEs are pre-exploit indicators — the host running an affected version is the necessary precondition for exploitation, even when no public PoC has been tested against this specific deployment.
findings.remediation_brief: Patch the SSH server to a release that fixes the CVE. For OpenSSH, upgrade via the operating system package manager (apt / dnf / pkg / yum). For embedded SSH stacks (Dropbear, Tectia, network appliances), apply vendor firmware updates. Where patching is not immediately feasible, restrict SSH access to trusted source IPs via firewall and monitor authentication logs for exploit attempts.

findings.title: SSH Configuration: Algorithm Hardening
findings.description: ssh-audit reports informational-severity recommendations for the SSH server's algorithm configuration. These are not vulnerabilities but represent opportunities to harden the configuration further by adding modern algorithms or removing older but still-secure ones.
findings.impact: No direct impact at this severity. Addressing these recommendations improves the long-term cryptographic posture of the SSH service and reduces the surface for future downgrade or algorithm-confusion attacks as cryptographic best-practice evolves.
findings.remediation_brief: Review the ssh-audit recommendations in the Output field. Update sshd_config (or vendor-equivalent) to add the recommended modern algorithms (e.g. sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com, curve25519-sha256) and remove deprecated algorithms not required for legacy client compatibility. Restart sshd and re-run ssh-audit to confirm the recommendations have been resolved.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: VNC: No Authentication Required
findings.remediation_brief: Configure VNC to require strong authentication. Use VNC password authentication at minimum; prefer certificate-based or OS-integrated authentication. Restrict VNC access to trusted networks via firewall rules and VPN.
findings.description: The VNC server accepts connections with security type 1 (None), allowing any remote user to connect without providing credentials. The RFB handshake confirms authentication is not enforced.
findings.impact: An attacker gains full interactive desktop access to the host without any credentials, enabling complete control of the system including file access, application execution, and keystroke capture.

findings.title: Discovery: VNC: Authentication Required But Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict VNC access to trusted networks. Consider disabling VNC if not required or replacing with a more secure remote access solution.
findings.description: A VNC service is accessible on the network and requires authentication. While authentication is enforced, the service is reachable for brute-force attacks.
findings.impact: VNC is reachable on the network, providing a target for credential brute-force attacks and potential exploitation of VNC implementation vulnerabilities.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: WinRM: No Authentication Required
findings.remediation_brief: Configure WinRM to require authentication (Kerberos or NTLM). Restrict WinRM access via Windows Firewall or GPO to trusted management networks only.
findings.description: The WinRM (Windows Remote Management) service responded to an unauthenticated SOAP/WS-Management request without requiring credentials, allowing remote command execution.
findings.impact: An attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the Windows host remotely without credentials, enabling full system compromise, data exfiltration, and lateral movement.

findings.title: Discovery: WinRM Service
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict WinRM access to trusted management networks via firewall rules. Disable WinRM if not operationally required.
findings.description: The WinRM service is active and responding on the network. Authentication is required but the service is reachable as an attack surface.
findings.impact: WinRM exposure provides a lateral movement target for attackers with valid credentials. Authentication methods exposed in WWW-Authenticate may guide attack strategy.

findings.title: Insecure Protocol Detected: WinRM (Cleartext)
findings.remediation_brief: Configure WinRM to use HTTPS (port 5986) with a valid TLS certificate. Disable the HTTP listener on port 5985.
findings.description: WinRM is running on port 5985 (HTTP) without TLS encryption. Administrative credentials are transmitted in cleartext or weakly encoded over the network.
findings.impact: An attacker on the network path can intercept WinRM credentials via packet capture, enabling remote command execution on the managed host.

findings.title: Insecure Protocol Detected: Telnet Service Exposed — Cleartext Protocol
findings.remediation_brief: Disable Telnet and replace with SSH for remote administration. If Telnet is operationally required, restrict access to trusted networks and monitor sessions.
findings.description: A Telnet service is exposed on the network. Telnet transmits all data including credentials in cleartext, making it trivially interceptable.
findings.impact: All data transmitted via Telnet, including usernames and passwords, can be captured by any attacker with network access. This enables credential theft and subsequent unauthorized access.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Kubernetes API: Unauthenticated Access
findings.remediation_brief: Enable RBAC and configure API server authentication (certificates, OIDC, or webhook). Restrict API access to authorized networks. Never expose the API server to untrusted networks.
findings.description: The Kubernetes API server is accessible without authentication. Unauthenticated requests can list, create, and modify cluster resources including pods, secrets, and deployments.
findings.impact: An attacker can fully compromise the Kubernetes cluster — deploying malicious containers, exfiltrating secrets (including cloud credentials and TLS keys), pivoting to other infrastructure, and achieving persistent backdoor access.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Kubelet API: Unauthenticated Access
findings.remediation_brief: Enable kubelet authentication and authorization (--authentication-token-webhook, --authorization-mode=Webhook). Disable the read-only port (10255).
findings.description: The Kubelet API on port 10250 is accessible without authentication, allowing direct interaction with containers running on the node.
findings.impact: An attacker can list running pods, execute commands inside containers, and exfiltrate data from any container on the node without any credentials.

findings.title: Discovery: Kubernetes API Endpoint Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure the Kubernetes API is not exposed to untrusted networks. Verify RBAC is properly configured.
findings.description: A Kubernetes API endpoint was detected on the network. Authentication is enforced but the endpoint's presence confirms a Kubernetes deployment.
findings.impact: Confirms Kubernetes infrastructure for further targeted attacks. Version information may aid CVE exploitation.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Rsync: Anonymous Module Access
findings.remediation_brief: Configure rsync modules to require authentication (auth users + secrets file). Restrict access by IP via hosts allow/deny. Disable rsync if not required.
findings.description: The rsync daemon allows anonymous listing and potentially read/write access to shared modules without authentication.
findings.impact: An attacker can enumerate and download files from shared rsync modules, potentially accessing configuration files, credentials, source code, or sensitive data. Write access enables malware deployment.

findings.title: Network Misconfiguration: Java RMI Registry Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict RMI registry access to localhost or trusted networks via firewall rules. Implement JMX authentication. Use serialization filters (JEP 290) to prevent deserialization attacks.
findings.description: A Java RMI registry is exposed on the network. The JRMI handshake was confirmed. Exposed RMI registries are vulnerable to deserialization attacks via ysoserial payloads.
findings.impact: An attacker can exploit Java deserialization vulnerabilities to achieve remote code execution on the server. Exposed RMI registries are a well-known exploitation vector with readily available tooling.

findings.title: Memcached: Unauthenticated Access
findings.remediation_brief: Enable SASL authentication for Memcached. Bind to localhost or trusted interfaces only. Implement firewall rules to restrict access. Consider Memcached with TLS (1.5.13+).
findings.description: Memcached is accessible without authentication. The 'stats' command returned data successfully, confirming no authentication is configured.
findings.impact: An attacker can read and modify cached data (including session tokens, credentials, and application data), flush the cache to cause a denial of service, or use the server for DDoS amplification attacks.

findings.title: Elasticsearch: Unauthenticated Access
findings.remediation_brief: Enable Elasticsearch security features (X-Pack Security or OpenSearch Security). Configure TLS and role-based access control. Bind to localhost or trusted interfaces only.
findings.description: Elasticsearch is accessible without authentication. Cluster health, indices, and all stored data can be queried and modified by any network-accessible client.
findings.impact: An attacker can read, modify, or delete all indexed data which may include PII, credentials, logs, and business-critical information. The cluster can also be used as a data exfiltration staging point.

findings.title: IoT: MQTT Broker: No Authentication Required
findings.remediation_brief: Enable MQTT authentication with username/password or client certificates. Configure ACLs to restrict topic access per client. Enable TLS encryption.
findings.description: The MQTT broker accepted a CONNECT packet without credentials (CONNACK return code 0x00), confirming no authentication is required.
findings.impact: An attacker can subscribe to all topics to intercept sensitive IoT/SCADA telemetry data, and publish malicious messages to manipulate connected devices or trigger unsafe actuator commands.

findings.title: IoT: MQTT Broker Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Verify MQTT broker authentication and ACLs are properly configured. Ensure TLS is enabled for production deployments.
findings.description: An MQTT broker was detected on the network. Authentication is enforced (CONNACK rejected unauthenticated connection).
findings.impact: Confirms an MQTT deployment for further targeted testing. The broker may be part of IoT or SCADA infrastructure.

findings.title: Authentication: Default Credentials Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Change or delete the default guest account immediately. Create named accounts with strong passwords and least-privilege permissions. Restrict management UI access to trusted networks.
findings.description: The RabbitMQ management UI is accessible with default credentials (guest/guest). The management API returned cluster overview data confirming full administrative access.
findings.impact: An attacker gains full administrative control of the message broker — able to read, modify, and delete message queues, create new users, access published messages containing potentially sensitive data, and disrupt message-dependent applications.

findings.title: Admin Endpoint Exposed: RabbitMQ
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict RabbitMQ management UI access to trusted management networks. Ensure strong authentication is configured.
findings.description: The RabbitMQ management UI on port 15672 is accessible on the network. Default credentials were rejected, indicating custom authentication is in place.
findings.impact: The management interface is a brute-force target. Successful authentication provides full administrative control of the message broker.

findings.title: Discovery: AMQP Service Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Verify AMQP authentication is properly configured. Restrict AMQP access to authorized clients only.
findings.description: An AMQP service was detected on port 5672. The protocol header exchange confirmed the service accepts AMQP 0-9-1 connections.
findings.impact: Confirms message broker infrastructure for further targeted testing.

findings.title: Insecure Protocol Detected: POP3: STARTTLS Not Supported
findings.remediation_brief: Enable STARTTLS on the POP3 server or migrate to POP3S (port 995). Ensure TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites.
findings.description: The POP3 server on port 110 does not advertise STLS capability in its CAPA response, meaning email retrieval credentials are transmitted in cleartext.
findings.impact: Email credentials transmitted over POP3 without TLS can be intercepted by any attacker on the network path, enabling unauthorized mailbox access.

findings.title: Insecure Protocol Detected: IMAP: STARTTLS Not Supported
findings.remediation_brief: Enable STARTTLS on the IMAP server or migrate to IMAPS (port 993). Ensure TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites.
findings.description: The IMAP server on port 143 does not advertise STARTTLS capability in its CAPABILITY response, meaning email credentials are transmitted in cleartext.
findings.impact: Email credentials transmitted over IMAP without TLS can be intercepted by any attacker on the network path, enabling unauthorized mailbox and email content access.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Cloud Metadata Endpoint Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Implement IMDSv2 (AWS) requiring session tokens. Block outbound access to 169.254.169.254 from application containers. Implement network policies restricting metadata endpoint access.
findings.description: The cloud instance metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) is accessible from an internal web service, indicating potential SSRF vulnerability or misconfigured network controls.
findings.impact: An attacker can extract cloud IAM temporary credentials, enabling full compromise of the cloud environment — lateral movement to other cloud services, data exfiltration from S3/Blob/GCS, and privilege escalation.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Jenkins: Unauthenticated Groovy Console (RCE)

mitre_attack.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain

findings.remediation_brief: Immediately restrict access to the Jenkins Script Console (/script) by configuring authentication. Enable Jenkins security realm and authorization strategy. Restrict access by IP at the network level.
findings.description: The Jenkins Groovy Script Console at /script is accessible without authentication, allowing execution of arbitrary Groovy code on the Jenkins server.
findings.impact: An attacker achieves immediate remote code execution on the Jenkins server. This enables reading credentials from the Jenkins credential store, modifying CI/CD pipelines for supply chain attacks, pivoting to build targets, and establishing persistent backdoors.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Jenkins: Unauthenticated Management Console
findings.remediation_brief: Configure Jenkins authentication and authorization. Restrict /manage access to authenticated administrators only. Enable a security realm.
findings.description: The Jenkins management console at /manage is accessible without authentication, exposing system configuration, plugin management, and credential stores.
findings.impact: An attacker can view and modify system configuration, install malicious plugins, access stored credentials, and manipulate build infrastructure.

findings.title: Active Directory: Kerberoastable Service Accounts Identified
findings.remediation_brief: Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) with automatically rotated 120-character passwords. For legacy SPNs, enforce 25+ character passwords. Use AES256 encryption for Kerberos tickets. Monitor for TGS-REQ anomalies.
findings.description: Service accounts with registered Service Principal Names (SPNs) were identified via Kerberos TGS-REP ticket requests. The extracted TGS tickets are crackable offline.
findings.impact: An attacker can request TGS tickets for SPN-registered service accounts and crack them offline with hashcat/john. Compromised service accounts often have elevated privileges, enabling domain privilege escalation.

findings.title: LDAP: Anonymous Enumeration — Users and Groups Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Disable anonymous LDAP binds. Configure the domain controller to require authenticated binds (dsHeuristics). Implement network segmentation to restrict LDAP access to authorized clients.
findings.description: LDAP anonymous bind is permitted and was used to enumerate Active Directory users, groups, and password policies. User/group data was extracted without credentials.
findings.impact: An attacker obtains a complete user and group listing for targeted attacks: password spraying, social engineering, and identifying privileged accounts. Password policy details inform brute-force strategy.

findings.title: SMB Vulnerability: SMBv3 Remote Code Execution (CVE-2020-0796)
findings.remediation_brief: Apply Microsoft security update KB4551762 immediately. Disable SMBv3 compression as a temporary mitigation via PowerShell: Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters' DisableCompression -Type DWORD -Value 1.
findings.description: The host is vulnerable to CVE-2020-0796 (SMBGhost), a buffer overflow in SMBv3 compression handling in Windows 10 (1903/1909) and Server 2019. Detected via nmap smb-vuln-cve-2020-0796 NSE script.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated attacker can achieve remote code execution with SYSTEM privileges via a specially crafted SMBv3 compressed packet. This is a wormable vulnerability — no user interaction required.

findings.title: Authentication: Default Credentials Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Change all FTP credentials from factory defaults to strong, unique passwords. Disable unnecessary FTP accounts. Consider replacing FTP with SFTP (SSH file transfer) for encrypted credential transmission.
findings.description: The FTP service accepted well-known default or factory-set credentials, granting authenticated access to the file transfer service.
findings.impact: An attacker with knowledge of default credentials can authenticate to the FTP service, potentially reading sensitive files, uploading malicious content, or using the server as a staging point for lateral movement. Default credentials are among the first things attackers test and are trivially discoverable.

findings.title: Authentication: FTP Brute Force Protection Not Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the FTP server to enforce connection rate limiting and account lockout after a threshold of failed login attempts. Most FTP servers (vsftpd, ProFTPD, Pure-FTPd) support MaxLoginAttempts or equivalent directives. Consider fail2ban as an additional layer.
findings.description: The FTP server did not exhibit rate limiting, account lockout, or connection throttling after multiple rapid failed login attempts.
findings.impact: Without brute-force protection, an attacker can make unlimited credential guessing attempts against the FTP service at high speed. This significantly reduces the time required to compromise accounts through dictionary attacks or credential stuffing.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Internal IP in HTTP Response
aliases: RFC 1918 Address Leakage in HTTP Response
findings.description: The HTTP response body or headers from a web service contain one or more RFC 1918 private IP addresses (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16). This reveals internal network topology to external observers.
findings.impact: An attacker can map internal network topology, identify backend hosts behind load balancers or proxies, and use disclosed addresses to craft targeted attacks such as SSRF against internal hosts or lateral movement after initial compromise.
findings.remediation_brief: Configure web servers and application frameworks to suppress internal IP addresses from HTTP responses. Review error pages, debug output, reverse proxy headers, and application-generated content for private address leakage.

findings.title: Discovery: Default Webpage Detected
findings.description: The website shows indicators of being outdated, abandoned, or unnecessary, such as old copyright dates, under-construction messages, or default server landing pages.
findings.impact: Outdated websites may contain unpatched vulnerabilities, deprecated frameworks, or unnecessary attack surface that increases the organization's risk profile.
findings.remediation_brief: Remove or decommission unnecessary websites. Update outdated content and frameworks. Replace default server pages with proper content or restrict access.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated Docker API Exposed
findings.description: The Docker Engine API is accessible without authentication. Endpoints such as /v1.24/containers/json and /v1.24/images/json return data freely, allowing enumeration of all containers and images on the host.
findings.impact: An attacker can create, start, stop, and delete containers, pull arbitrary images, mount the host filesystem via --privileged containers, read secrets and environment variables from running containers, and achieve full host-level remote code execution.
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict Docker API access to localhost or trusted networks. Enable TLS client certificate authentication. Use Docker's built-in authorization plugins.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass: PostgreSQL Trust Authentication Enabled
findings.description: PostgreSQL accepts connections as user 'postgres' without requiring a password, indicating trust authentication is configured in pg_hba.conf for the connecting network.
findings.impact: Full superuser database access to anyone who can reach the port, allowing data exfiltration, modification, deletion, and potential OS command execution via COPY TO PROGRAM or custom functions.
findings.remediation_brief: Reconfigure pg_hba.conf to require md5, scram-sha-256, or certificate authentication for all connections. Remove any 'trust' entries for non-local connections.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated CouchDB Access
findings.description: CouchDB allows unauthenticated access to the /_all_dbs endpoint, revealing the list of all databases on the server.
findings.impact: An attacker can enumerate all databases, read sensitive data, modify or delete documents, and potentially achieve remote code execution via CouchDB's query server functionality.
findings.remediation_brief: Configure CouchDB to require authentication for all endpoints. Set require_valid_user = true in the [chttpd] section of local.ini.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Grafana Unauthenticated API Access
findings.description: Grafana allows unauthenticated access to API endpoints such as /api/org, exposing organization details, dashboards, and data sources.
findings.impact: Attackers can view dashboards containing sensitive metrics, enumerate data source configurations (which may include database credentials), and access alerting rules. Anonymous API access can also be leveraged to discover internal infrastructure.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable anonymous access in grafana.ini by setting [auth.anonymous] enabled = false. Implement authentication for all API endpoints.

findings.title: Authentication: Default Credentials Accepted
findings.description: Grafana accepts the default credentials admin:admin, granting full administrative access to the Grafana instance.
findings.impact: Full administrative access to all dashboards, data sources (which may contain database credentials and API keys), alerting rules, user management, and the ability to install plugins that could provide further access to the underlying system.
findings.remediation_brief: Change the default admin password immediately. Enforce strong password policies and consider implementing SSO/LDAP authentication.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated Kibana Access
findings.description: Kibana exposes its /api/status endpoint without authentication, revealing version information and system status. Full unauthenticated access may also allow reading Elasticsearch indices.
findings.impact: Attackers can read Elasticsearch indices containing logs, metrics, and potentially sensitive data. Version disclosure enables targeted vulnerability exploitation. Kibana Dev Tools can be used to execute arbitrary Elasticsearch queries.
findings.remediation_brief: Enable X-Pack security or Elastic Stack security features. Configure authentication for all Kibana endpoints. Use a reverse proxy with authentication as an additional layer.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Cassandra Unauthenticated CQL Access
aliases: Cassandra Native Protocol Accessible Without Authentication
findings.description: Cassandra CQL accepted a STARTUP frame and returned READY without requesting authentication, indicating the PasswordAuthenticator is not enabled.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated read/write access to all keyspaces and tables. An attacker can exfiltrate data, modify records, create or drop keyspaces, and potentially affect cluster stability.
findings.remediation_brief: Enable PasswordAuthenticator in cassandra.yaml. Create administrative users with strong passwords and configure role-based access control.

findings.title: Sensitive File Exposed: Git Repository Exposed via Web
findings.description: The web server exposes a .git directory. The /.git/HEAD file returns a valid Git ref, indicating the full repository is accessible.
findings.impact: An attacker can reconstruct the complete source code repository including all commit history, which may contain hardcoded credentials, API keys, database connection strings, internal comments revealing business logic, and configuration for other internal systems.
findings.remediation_brief: Block access to .git directories in the web server configuration (e.g., Apache: <DirectoryMatch "\.git"> Deny from all </DirectoryMatch>). Deploy without the .git directory or use .gitignore and deployment pipelines.

findings.title: Web Misconfiguration: Unsafe Methods Enabled
findings.description: The web server allows dangerous HTTP methods such as PUT, DELETE, MOVE, COPY, or PROPFIND as reported by the OPTIONS response Allow header.
findings.impact: PUT can allow arbitrary file upload (including web shells), DELETE can remove files, MOVE/COPY enable WebDAV file manipulation, and PROPFIND discloses directory structure and metadata. These methods may enable remote code execution or data destruction.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable unused HTTP methods in the web server configuration. For Apache: use LimitExcept directive. For Nginx: return 405 for non-GET/POST methods.

findings.title: Web Misconfiguration: Unsafe Methods Enabled
findings.description: The web server responds to HTTP TRACE requests by echoing the full request back, including all headers.
findings.impact: The TRACE method can be exploited for Cross-Site Tracing (XST) attacks, which combine XSS with TRACE to steal HTTP authentication credentials and cookies even when HttpOnly is set.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable the TRACE method in the web server configuration. Apache: TraceEnable Off. Nginx: does not support TRACE by default.

findings.title: Sensitive File Exposed: {_status_label} Page Exposed
findings.description: The Apache server-status or server-info page is publicly accessible, exposing detailed server information including version, uptime, active connections, client IPs, and request URIs.
findings.impact: Reveals internal IP addresses, active request URIs (which may contain session tokens or API keys), client connections, server configuration details, and loaded modules. This information facilitates targeted exploitation.
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict access to mod_status and mod_info via Apache configuration (<Location /server-status> Require local </Location>) or disable them entirely.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Internal Hostname in HTTP Response
findings.description: The HTTP response contains internal hostnames matching common internal TLD patterns (.local, .internal, .corp, .lan, .intranet, .private, .home, .localdomain).
findings.impact: Internal hostname disclosure reveals the internal naming convention, domain structure, environment names (dev/staging/prod), and infrastructure layout. This aids reconnaissance and social engineering attacks.
findings.remediation_brief: Remove internal hostnames from HTTP response headers, error pages, and application output. Use generic external-facing hostnames.

findings.title: Debug Endpoint Exposed: {_dbg_label}
findings.description: A debug or management endpoint (e.g., /actuator, /actuator/env, /debug, /__debug__, /console) is accessible and returns diagnostic information.
findings.impact: Debug endpoints expose environment variables (which may contain credentials and API keys), database connection strings, application configuration, stack traces, and internal application state. Spring Boot Actuator /env can reveal secrets; H2 Console at /console can enable SQL injection.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable debug endpoints in production environments. For Spring Boot: restrict actuator endpoints via management.endpoints.web.exposure.include. For Django: set DEBUG=False.

findings.title: Sensitive File Exposed: PHP Info Page Exposed
findings.description: A phpinfo() page is accessible, exposing the complete PHP configuration including loaded modules, file paths, environment variables, and server details.
findings.impact: phpinfo() reveals the full server configuration, PHP version, loaded extensions, environment variables (which may contain database passwords and API keys), file paths, and operating system details. This enables targeted exploitation of known PHP and module vulnerabilities.
findings.remediation_brief: Remove phpinfo files from production servers. Disable the phpinfo() function via php.ini: disable_functions = phpinfo.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: DNS Server Version Disclosed
aliases: DNS Server Version Disclosed via CHAOS Query
findings.description: The DNS server discloses its version string via a CHAOS TXT query for version.bind.
findings.impact: Software version disclosure enables attackers to identify known vulnerabilities for the specific DNS server version and craft targeted exploits. BIND version disclosure is a common reconnaissance target.
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the DNS server to suppress or fake version responses. For BIND: options { version "none"; }; For PowerDNS: server-id and version-string settings.

findings.title: Enumeration: SMTP Mailing List Enumeration via EXPN
findings.description: The SMTP EXPN command is enabled and reveals mailing list membership, disclosing valid email addresses and group membership.
findings.impact: EXPN reveals valid email addresses and organizational group membership, enabling targeted phishing campaigns, social engineering, and password-spray attacks. Combined with VRFY, it provides a comprehensive user enumeration capability.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses

findings.remediation_brief: Disable the SMTP EXPN command or restrict it to authenticated sessions. In Postfix: smtpd_expansion_filter. In Sendmail: PrivacyOptions=noexpn.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Hostname Mismatch
findings.description: The SSL/TLS certificate Common Name (CN) does not match the hostname used to connect, as reported by testssl.sh.
findings.impact: A hostname mismatch causes browsers and clients to display security warnings. Users may learn to ignore these warnings, making them vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. The mismatch may also indicate a misconfigured or reused certificate.
findings.remediation_brief: Obtain a certificate that matches the server hostname in the CN or SAN fields. Use wildcard certificates for multiple subdomains.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Sensitive Path in robots.txt
findings.description: The robots.txt file contains Disallow entries for potentially sensitive paths such as admin panels, backup directories, configuration files, or development endpoints.
findings.impact: While robots.txt instructs well-behaved crawlers to skip listed paths, it simultaneously advertises them to attackers. Sensitive paths in robots.txt serve as a roadmap for targeted enumeration and exploitation.
findings.remediation_brief: Review robots.txt entries for sensitive paths. Remove entries that disclose internal structure. Ensure listed paths require authentication regardless of robots.txt.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Internal Hostname in SAN
findings.description: The SSL/TLS certificate includes internal hostnames in its Subject Alternative Names, matching patterns like .local, .internal, .corp, .lan, .intranet, .private.
findings.impact: Internal hostnames in publicly accessible certificates disclose the internal naming scheme, domain structure, and potentially the existence of internal services. This aids network mapping and targeted attacks against internal infrastructure.
findings.remediation_brief: Remove internal hostnames from the SAN list in certificates used on public-facing services. Use separate certificates for internal and external services.

findings.title: Network Misconfiguration: UPnP/SSDP Service Responding
findings.description: The UPnP/SSDP service responded to an M-SEARCH discovery request, revealing device information and service endpoints.
findings.impact: UPnP can expose device details and allow port forwarding changes without authentication. SSDP has been used in large-scale DDoS amplification attacks. Device information aids targeted exploitation of known firmware vulnerabilities.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable UPnP if not required. Restrict SSDP (UDP 1900) via firewall rules to trusted networks only. Disable UPnP on routers and IoT devices.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: MongoDB Unauthenticated Access
findings.description: MongoDB accepted an isMaster query via the native OP_QUERY protocol without requiring authentication, indicating authorization is not enabled.
findings.impact: Full read/write access to all databases, allowing data exfiltration, modification, deletion, and user creation. MongoDB instances without auth have been widely targeted by ransomware campaigns that delete databases and demand payment.
findings.remediation_brief: Enable authorization in mongod.conf (security.authorization: enabled). Create administrative users with strong passwords. Bind MongoDB to localhost or trusted interfaces only.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Directory Listing Enabled
findings.description: The web server has directory listing enabled, displaying file names, sizes, and modification dates to anyone who requests a directory without an index file.
findings.impact: Directory listings allow attackers to discover backup files, configuration files, source code, database dumps, and other sensitive content that would otherwise require blind enumeration.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable directory listing in the web server configuration. Apache: Options -Indexes. Nginx: autoindex off.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Certificate: Not Trusted
findings.description: The SSL/TLS certificate is not trusted by common certificate stores, as reported by testssl.sh. This may indicate a self-signed certificate, an expired certificate, or a certificate from an untrusted CA.
findings.impact: Untrusted certificates cause browser warnings that users learn to ignore, making them vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. This may also indicate an attacker-controlled certificate or a certificate from a compromised CA.
findings.remediation_brief: Obtain a certificate from a trusted Certificate Authority. Ensure the full certificate chain is properly configured on the server.

findings.title: SSL/TLS Forward Secrecy: Not Supported
findings.description: The server does not offer any cipher suites with forward secrecy (ECDHE or DHE key exchange). Without forward secrecy, compromise of the server's private key allows retroactive decryption of all recorded past sessions.
findings.impact: An attacker who obtains the server's private key (through theft, legal compulsion, or future cryptanalysis) can decrypt all previously captured TLS traffic. Forward secrecy ensures each session uses ephemeral keys that are discarded, making past sessions safe even if the long-term key is compromised.
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the server to use only cipher suites that provide forward secrecy (ECDHE or DHE key exchange). Disable static RSA key exchange. TLSv1.3 mandates forward secrecy and should be preferred.

findings.title: SSH Configuration: Password Authentication Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable PasswordAuthentication and ChallengeResponseAuthentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Require public key authentication exclusively. CIS Benchmark and DISA STIG both mandate disabling password-based SSH login.
findings.description: The SSH server accepts password-based authentication methods (password and/or keyboard-interactive) alongside public key authentication. Password authentication is susceptible to brute-force attacks and does not enforce multi-factor authentication.
findings.impact: An attacker can attempt password brute-force attacks against the SSH service. Even with strong passwords, password authentication lacks the cryptographic assurance of key-based authentication and is incompatible with most MFA implementations. Compliance frameworks including CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs mandate public-key-only SSH authentication.

findings.title: SSH Configuration: Password Authentication Only
findings.remediation_brief: Enable public key authentication and disable PasswordAuthentication and ChallengeResponseAuthentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Generate and deploy SSH key pairs for all authorized users. CIS Benchmark and DISA STIG both mandate public-key-only SSH login.
findings.description: The SSH server accepts only password-based authentication methods (password and/or keyboard-interactive) with no public key authentication available. This is a significant security weakness — the server cannot accept key-based authentication at all, making brute-force the only barrier to unauthorized access.
findings.impact: Without public key authentication, the SSH server relies entirely on password strength for security. An attacker can mount online brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks with no cryptographic barrier. The absence of public key support also prevents deployment of certificate-based or hardware-token SSH authentication. This configuration violates CIS Benchmark and DISA STIG requirements for SSH hardening.

findings.title: Discovery: O365 Tenant Detected
findings.description: The target domain uses Microsoft 365 / Azure AD for email and authentication. MX records point to *.protection.outlook.com or the OpenID configuration endpoint confirms an Azure AD tenant.
findings.impact: Confirms the organization uses Microsoft 365, enabling targeted O365 account enumeration, credential spray, and phishing attacks against the tenant.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses

findings.remediation_brief: Implement conditional access policies, enforce MFA, and configure Azure AD Smart Lockout to mitigate enumeration and credential spray attacks.

findings.title: Enumeration: O365 Account Enumeration
findings.description: Valid O365 user accounts were confirmed via Azure AD authentication endpoint enumeration. The endpoint returns different responses for valid and invalid accounts, allowing an attacker to confirm which email addresses correspond to active accounts.
findings.impact: Confirmed valid accounts can be targeted with password spray attacks, credential stuffing, phishing campaigns, and social engineering. This significantly reduces the attacker's search space for credential-based attacks.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses

findings.remediation_brief: Implement conditional access policies, enforce MFA on all accounts, configure Azure AD Smart Lockout, and disable legacy authentication protocols that bypass MFA. Monitor Azure AD sign-in logs for enumeration patterns.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated X11 Display Access
findings.description: An X11 display server accepts connections without authentication. The service responded to either xdpyinfo queries or raw X11 protocol handshake without requiring XAUTH/MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE credentials.
findings.impact: An attacker can capture screen contents in real-time, inject keystrokes and mouse events, monitor all user activity on the display, and potentially execute arbitrary commands through keystroke injection. This provides full visibility into and control over the user's desktop session.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable remote X11 connections or enforce XAUTH/MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE authentication. Configure X11 to listen only on localhost (-nolisten tcp). Use SSH X11 forwarding instead of direct X11 connections. Apply firewall rules to block ports 6000-6063 from untrusted networks.

findings.title: Discovery: X11 Display Detected (Authentication Required)
findings.description: An X11 display server is running but requires authentication to connect. The X11 protocol handshake was rejected with an authentication-required response.
findings.impact: The X11 service is exposed on the network but properly requires authentication. While the service itself is secured, exposure of X11 ports to untrusted networks increases the attack surface. If authentication credentials are weak or compromised, the display could be accessed remotely.
findings.remediation_brief: Verify X11 is configured to listen only on localhost unless remote access is required. Use SSH X11 forwarding instead of direct connections. Apply firewall rules to restrict access to X11 ports.

findings.title: Authentication: Default Credentials Accepted
findings.description: brutespray confirmed that a network service accepts default or factory-preset credentials. The service responded with a successful authentication using a well-known username/password combination.
findings.impact: An attacker can immediately authenticate to the service using widely-known default credentials. Depending on the service, this may provide full administrative access, ability to read/modify data, execute commands, pivot to other systems, or completely compromise the host. Default credentials are among the most commonly exploited vulnerabilities.
findings.remediation_brief: Change all default credentials immediately. Implement strong, unique passwords for all service accounts. Deploy account lockout policies. Consider disabling unnecessary services entirely.

findings.title: Authentication: Weak Credentials: {SERVICE}
findings.description: brutespray confirmed that a network service accepts weak or easily guessable credentials. The service authenticated successfully with a non-default but weak username/password combination.
findings.impact: An attacker can authenticate to the service using credentials that are easily guessable or present in common wordlists. This may provide unauthorized access to sensitive data, the ability to modify configurations, or a foothold for lateral movement within the network.
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce strong password policies with minimum length, complexity, and rotation requirements. Implement account lockout after failed attempts. Deploy multi-factor authentication where possible.

findings.title: OS Version Detected: {os} [Inferred]
findings.description: Operating system inferred from software version analysis and port fingerprinting rather than direct nmap OS detection or SSH banner identification. Inference sources include IIS version to Windows Server edition mapping, SQL Server version correlation, OpenSSH banner to Linux distribution mapping, Cockpit version to RHEL mapping, Microsoft service software presence, VMware ESXi detection, and Windows-characteristic port combinations (RDP, SMB, MSRPC, WinRM).
findings.impact: Accurate OS identification enables targeted vulnerability assessment, patch validation, and compliance scope determination. Inferred OS guides the tester toward OS-specific attack vectors, default credential databases, and known exploit chains. Without OS identification, vulnerability assessment is less targeted and may miss platform-specific weaknesses.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate inferred OS with targeted nmap -O scan or authenticated assessment. Use the inferred OS to scope platform-specific vulnerability checks.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Domain Controller
findings.description: Host identified as an Active Directory Domain Controller based on Kerberos (88/tcp), LDAP (389/tcp), and supporting services (Global Catalog, DNS, SMB). Domain Controllers are the central authentication and authorization authority for Windows Active Directory environments.
findings.impact: Domain Controllers hold the keys to the entire Active Directory environment. Compromise of a DC grants access to all domain-joined systems, user credentials (NTDS.dit), Group Policy Objects, and Kerberos ticket-granting services. DCs are prime targets for Kerberoasting, DCSync, Golden Ticket, and Pass-the-Hash attacks. Identifying DCs early directs the tester to the highest-value targets.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — DNS Server
findings.description: Host identified as a DNS server based on port 53 (TCP/UDP) and optionally detected DNS software (BIND, dnsmasq, Unbound, PowerDNS, Microsoft DNS).
findings.impact: DNS servers reveal internal network topology, naming conventions, and service locations through zone transfers (AXFR) and record enumeration. A compromised DNS server enables DNS poisoning, traffic redirection, and man-in-the-middle attacks across the entire network.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — DHCP Server
findings.description: Host identified as a DHCP server based on port 67/udp and optionally detected DHCP software (ISC DHCP, dnsmasq).
findings.impact: DHCP servers control IP address assignment and can push configuration to all clients including DNS servers, default gateways, and proxy settings. A rogue or compromised DHCP server enables network-wide man-in-the-middle attacks via malicious gateway or DNS injection.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Mail Server
findings.description: Host identified as a mail server based on SMTP (25/tcp) and optionally POP3/IMAP/submission ports (110, 143, 465, 587, 993, 995) with detected mail software (Postfix, Sendmail, Exim, Exchange, Dovecot).
findings.impact: Mail servers process and store organizational email containing sensitive communications, credentials, and attachments. They are targets for credential harvesting, phishing relay, open relay abuse, and data exfiltration. Exchange servers in particular may expose OWA and EWS interfaces with known exploitation chains (ProxyShell, ProxyLogon).
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Web Server
findings.description: Host identified as a web server based on HTTP/HTTPS ports (80, 443, 8080, 8443) and optionally detected web server software (Nginx, Apache, IIS, Tomcat, Lighttpd, Caddy, HAProxy).
findings.impact: Web servers host applications, APIs, and administrative interfaces that represent a significant portion of the external attack surface. Identification enables targeted web vulnerability scanning, technology-specific exploit testing, and web application penetration testing.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Database Server
findings.description: Host identified as a database server based on database ports (MySQL 3306, PostgreSQL 5432, MSSQL 1433, Oracle 1521, MongoDB 27017, Redis 6379, Cassandra 9042) and optionally detected database software.
findings.impact: Database servers store the organization's structured data including user records, financial data, and application state. Direct database access enables data exfiltration, privilege escalation via stored procedures, and lateral movement through linked servers or database links. Exposed database ports are high-value targets for credential brute-forcing.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — File Server
findings.description: Host identified as a file server based on SMB (445/tcp), NetBIOS (139/tcp), NFS (2049/tcp), and RPC (111/tcp) port combinations.
findings.impact: File servers contain shared documents, configuration files, scripts, and potentially credentials or sensitive data in accessible shares. SMB shares are prime targets for credential relay attacks (NTLM relay), sensitive data discovery, and lateral movement. NFS exports may allow unauthorized access when misconfigured.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Print Server
findings.description: Host identified as a print server based on IPP (631/tcp), LPD (515/tcp), or JetDirect (9100/tcp) ports and optionally CUPS software detection.
findings.impact: Print servers process documents that may contain sensitive information. Print protocols (IPP, LPD, JetDirect) historically have weak authentication and known vulnerabilities. CUPS servers may expose administrative interfaces and have been subject to remote code execution vulnerabilities.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Proxy/Load Balancer
findings.description: Host identified as a proxy or load balancer based on common proxy ports (3128, 8080, 8443) and optionally detected software (Squid, HAProxy, Nginx, Varnish, Envoy, Traefik, F5).
findings.impact: Proxy and load balancer infrastructure reveals backend server topology and may expose administrative interfaces. Misconfigured proxies can enable server-side request forgery (SSRF), cache poisoning, and access to internal-only services. Load balancer admin panels may grant control over traffic routing.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — VPN Gateway
findings.description: Host identified as a VPN gateway based on OpenVPN (1194/tcp/udp), IKE (500/udp), NAT-T (4500/udp), L2TP (1701/udp), or PPTP (1723/tcp) ports and optionally detected VPN software.
findings.impact: VPN gateways are the entry point to internal networks from external locations. Compromising a VPN gateway grants authenticated access to the internal network segment. VPN appliances have been subject to critical vulnerabilities (Pulse Secure, Fortinet, Cisco AnyConnect) that enable pre-authentication remote code execution.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — RADIUS Server
findings.description: Host identified as a RADIUS authentication server based on authentication (1812/udp) and accounting (1813/udp) ports and optionally detected RADIUS software (FreeRADIUS).
findings.impact: RADIUS servers centralize network access authentication for VPN, wireless, and 802.1X wired access. Compromising a RADIUS server enables authentication bypass for all connected network access infrastructure, potentially granting access to every network segment protected by 802.1X or VPN authentication.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Monitoring Server
findings.description: Host identified as a monitoring or observability server based on SNMP (161-162/udp), Prometheus (9090/tcp), Grafana (3000/tcp), Kibana (5601/tcp), or Elasticsearch (9200/tcp) port combinations and optionally detected monitoring software.
findings.impact: Monitoring servers aggregate telemetry, logs, and metrics from across the infrastructure, providing a comprehensive view of network topology, service health, and security events. Compromising a monitoring server reveals the full infrastructure map and may expose credentials stored in data source configurations. SNMP community strings and monitoring agent credentials are high-value targets.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Virtualization Host
findings.description: Host identified as a virtualization host based on VMware (902/tcp, 443/tcp), Proxmox (8006/tcp) ports and optionally detected hypervisor software (ESXi, VMware, Proxmox, vCenter).
findings.impact: Virtualization hosts run multiple virtual machines and represent high-value targets. Compromising a hypervisor grants access to all hosted VMs, their virtual disks, memory contents, and network traffic. ESXi and vCenter have been subject to critical vulnerabilities enabling remote code execution and VM escape.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.description: Host identified as a CI/CD server based on Jenkins (8080/tcp, 50000/tcp), GitLab, TeamCity, or Bamboo port and software detection.
findings.impact: CI/CD servers have access to source code repositories, build artifacts, deployment credentials, and production infrastructure. Compromising a CI/CD pipeline enables supply chain attacks, credential theft from build environments, and code injection into production deployments. Jenkins servers frequently expose unauthenticated script consoles.
