findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Container Host
findings.description: Host identified as a container orchestration host based on Docker API (2375-2376/tcp), Kubernetes API (6443/tcp), kubelet (10250/tcp) ports and optionally detected container software (Docker, Kubernetes, Portainer, Rancher).
findings.impact: Container hosts run containerized workloads and expose orchestration APIs that may grant cluster-wide access. An exposed Docker socket (2375/tcp without TLS) allows arbitrary container creation with host filesystem access. Kubernetes API access enables pod creation, secret extraction, and lateral movement across the cluster.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Identified — Backup Server
findings.description: Host identified as a backup server based on Veeam (10000/tcp), Bacula/Bareos (9103/tcp), or monitoring agent (6556/tcp) ports and optionally detected backup software.
findings.impact: Backup servers contain copies of data from across the infrastructure, including databases, file servers, and application data. Compromising a backup server provides access to historical data, potentially including credentials, and may enable restoration of data to attacker-controlled systems. Backup credentials often have broad read access across the environment.
findings.remediation_brief: Informational finding. Validate server role and ensure appropriate hardening per role. Apply role-specific security baselines (CIS benchmarks, DISA STIGs) and verify least-privilege network access.

findings.title: Software Detected: {_sw_label}
findings.description: Software product identified on a host without a specific version number. While the product name is known, the absence of version information limits vulnerability assessment.
findings.impact: Identified software presence reveals the technology stack in use. Without version information, targeted CVE matching is not possible, but the product category still aids attack surface mapping.
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict service banner exposure and unnecessary protocol responses to limit software fingerprinting opportunities.

findings.title: Discovery: Environment Tier Inferred — {environment}
findings.description: Server environment tier (e.g. Production, Test, DR, Pre-Production) inferred from hostname naming convention analysis.
findings.impact: Environment classification reveals network segmentation practices and identifies production systems that handle live data, aiding risk prioritization.
findings.remediation_brief: Review hostname naming conventions to ensure they do not inadvertently expose environment classification to unauthenticated users. Consider using opaque hostnames for externally-facing systems.

findings.title: Discovery: Application Identified — {app_name}
findings.description: Enterprise application identified from hostname naming convention. The hostname pattern matches a known product naming scheme.
findings.impact: Application identification from hostnames reveals the technology stack without requiring active probing, aiding targeted vulnerability research and attack surface mapping.
findings.remediation_brief: Use opaque hostnames that do not embed application or product names for internet-facing systems.

findings.title: Discovery: Hardware Model Identified — {model}
findings.description: Server hardware model inferred from hostname naming convention. The hostname contains a pattern matching a known server hardware model number.
findings.impact: Hardware model identification reveals the physical infrastructure platform, which may have known firmware vulnerabilities or BIOS/BMC attack surfaces (e.g., iDRAC, iLO).
findings.remediation_brief: Avoid embedding hardware model identifiers in hostnames. Review BIOS/firmware update status on identified hardware platforms.

findings.title: Discovery: Server Role Inferred — {role}
findings.description: Server role inferred from hostname token analysis. Keywords in the hostname suggest a specific server function (e.g., sql=Database, api=API Server, vpn=VPN Gateway).
findings.impact: Server role identification aids in targeting specific service types and identifying high-value targets such as database servers, domain controllers, or backup systems.
findings.remediation_brief: Use role-neutral hostnames for externally-facing systems. Ensure hostname-implied services are properly hardened for their role.

findings.title: SSH Configuration: Keyboard-Interactive Only (No Public Key)
findings.description: The SSH server accepts only keyboard-interactive authentication with no public key option. Keyboard-interactive may be PAM-based password prompts, TOTP/OTP, Duo push, or other challenge-response mechanisms. Without public key authentication available, the server relies entirely on challenge-response security.
findings.impact: Without public key authentication, the SSH server cannot accept key-based or certificate-based login. If the keyboard-interactive backend is password-based PAM, the server is susceptible to brute-force attacks. Even if the backend is 2FA, the absence of a public key option limits authentication flexibility and violates CIS/STIG hardening requirements.
findings.remediation_brief: Enable public key authentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. If keyboard-interactive is used for 2FA, ensure public key is also available as a primary authentication factor. Deploy SSH key pairs for all authorized users.

findings.title: Discovery: Live Host — No Services Exposed
findings.description: Host responded to discovery probes (confirmed alive) but no open TCP or UDP ports were identified. The majority of scanned ports returned RST (closed), indicating the host is genuinely reachable with no exposed services. It may be a network device, a hardened endpoint, or a host with services on non-standard ports outside the scanned range.
findings.impact: A live host with no exposed services still represents an asset on the network that must be inventoried. It may be running services accessible only via UDP or on non-standard ports not covered by the scan range. The host should be included in the asset inventory and evaluated for whether its presence on the network is expected.
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the host is expected on this network segment. If it is an unmanaged or unauthorized device, investigate and either decommission or bring under management. Ensure asset inventory reflects this host.

findings.title: Discovery: Live Host — Filtered (Possible Segmentation)
findings.description: Host responded to discovery probes (confirmed alive) but 90% or more of scanned ports are filtered — probes received no response, indicating a firewall or ACL is actively dropping traffic to this host. When an entire subnet exhibits this behavior while adjacent subnets respond normally, it is strong evidence of network segmentation enforcement.
findings.impact: A host behind a fully-filtered firewall indicates active access control enforcement at the network layer. This is a positive security control when intentional (segmentation between VLANs, DMZ boundaries, production/test isolation). Compare against other scanned subnets to map segmentation boundaries. If segmentation is expected, this confirms the control is operating. If unexpected, it may indicate misconfigured ACLs blocking legitimate traffic or an undocumented security zone.
findings.remediation_brief: No remediation required if segmentation is intentional. Document the segmentation boundary and verify it aligns with the network architecture diagram. If the host should be accessible from the scan source, investigate firewall rules or ACLs that may be blocking traffic.
